A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeepLTL research and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Renumbered and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments in LetterWorld, ZoneEnv, and FlatWorld, including finite- and infinite-horizon tasks, baseline comparisons, and supplementary analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds architecture, proposition-count, specification-complexity, and RAD-embeddings evaluations in Appendix G.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes its accepting-cycle test: v1 propagates a Boolean accepting flag, whereas v2 tracks the last accepting state's index and checks whether it lies within the closed cycle. This is a localized procedural correction. The DeepSets/GRU architecture, training rewards, and value-based sequence selection remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The three original environments remain, but v2 materially extends tested task requirements with a parity task explicitly outside LTL. Appendices G.6-G.8 also add modified FlatWorld environments with 8-20 atomic propositions and tests involving larger automata and demanding avoidance conditions.

E2.justification: Table 8 adds RAD-embeddings as an evaluated external comparator, including comparisons on the existing ZoneEnv specifications φ6-φ11. The original LTL2Action and GCRL-LTL comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce a controlled GRU-to-Transformer substitution, fixed architecture across proposition-count variants, and RAD evaluation using frozen pretrained GATv2 embeddings with 15M interaction steps. The original PPO settings and evaluation metrics remain. FlatWorld's stated state space changes from R² to [-2,2]²; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained curriculum ablation, adversarial safety test, and long-sequence analysis, v2 adds a sequence-module ablation, proposition-count sensitivity analysis, and specification-complexity case studies. These investigate architecture choice, scaling, and why large formulas can succeed while simpler avoidance-heavy tasks remain difficult.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-seed evaluations, standard deviations in result tables, and 90% confidence intervals in plots. The added studies use these existing reporting practices; no revised uncertainty procedure or increased run count for retained experiments is reported.

E6.justification: Original benchmark values are retained, but substantial results are added. Table 7 reports φ7 success rates of 0.46 for the Transformer variant versus 0.91 for GRU. Table 8 finds broadly similar success rates against RAD-embeddings with fewer DeepLTL steps, and higher success on large1/large2. New analyses report proposition-count trends and 98% versus 82% success on two different complexity case studies.

T1.justification: Theorem 1, Lemma 1, their proof, and the formal LTL and product-MDP definitions retain their mathematical substance. The eventual-discounting objective moves into Appendix B with notation changes. New Appendix C discusses connections to discounted LTL without adding a formal derivation or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the central claims: zero-shot LTL execution, non-myopic planning, infinite-horizon support, safety-aware representations, and empirical effectiveness. Explicit multi-task wording clarifies the existing setting; removing the novelty hedge does not establish a different scientific contribution.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations and applicability boundaries. It discusses why short sequences favor GRUs, how failure to learn individual propositions affects compound tasks, and why environment dynamics matter more than formula size alone. It explicitly acknowledges infeasible LDBA construction in the worst case and discusses applicability beyond LTL and the nuanced RAD comparison.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link in the abstract and documents the new Transformer configuration, including embedding size, attention heads, MLP size, and dropout. It also specifies RAD's frozen pretrained embeddings and training procedure. Existing architecture, PPO, and curriculum details are largely retained.

R1.justification: Section 6 and new Appendices C-D substantially expand positioning against single-task RL, task-generalizing methods, discounted LTL, and automata-conditioned RL. Added discussions include Yalcinkaya et al., Almagor et al., and Alur et al.; v2 also explicitly acknowledges the accepting-cycle algorithm's relationship to Shah et al.

P1.justification: v2 updates the title and publication header, streamlines Section 3, relocates the eventual-discounting formulation, expands appendix organization, and revises the conclusion. The main section sequence and most existing method and experimental prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 7-8 and the two-panel Figure 11 using the existing visual style. Existing appendix displays move, trajectory figures are renumbered, Figure 1's panel reference is corrected, and Table 6 gains metric-direction arrows. The original diagrams, plots, and table structures are largely preserved.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of central design choices through the Transformer ablation and RAD-embeddings comparison, while the scaling and complexity studies expose practical limits missing from v1. Corrected accepting-cycle pseudocode and added code-access information improve technical usefulness. These changes address important gaps in architectural justification, comparative evidence, and applicability boundaries; the original benchmark results remain unchanged.
